main.title: UC Berkeley CS 168: Introduction to the Internet
main.why: Layers, routing and BGP, TCP and congestion control, DNS and HTTP, then datacenters and SDN. In English.

main.title: End-to-End Arguments in System Design
main.why: Why reliability and correctness belong at the endpoints, the argument behind a simple network core.

main.title: The Design Philosophy of the DARPA Internet Protocols
main.why: The Internet's goals in priority order, and how that order produced datagrams, TCP/IP layering and weak accounting.

main.title: Development of the Domain Name System
main.why: A single hosts file could not keep up with the growing Internet, so DNS delegates names to a hierarchy of zones served with caching resolvers.

main.title: A Detailed Look at RFC 8446 (a.k.a. TLS 1.3)
main.why: TLS 1.3 shortens the handshake, adds 0-RTT resumption with its replay risk, and removes the legacy crypto behind past attacks.

main.title: Congestion Avoidance and Control
main.why: After the Internet's congestion collapse, slow start, AIMD and RTT estimation made TCP back off when the network fills.
Loss is a poor congestion signal on deep buffers, so BBR paces to measured bandwidth and RTT instead.

main.title: The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment
main.why: TCP and TLS cost extra round trips and stall every stream on a loss, so Google's pre-IETF QUIC runs transport and crypto over UDP in userspace.

main.title: How Facebook is bringing QUIC to billions
main.why: Meta moved its apps to IETF QUIC on its own implementation, and had to retune app heuristics that assumed TCP.

main.title: Engineering Egress with Edge Fabric: Steering Oceans of Content to the World
main.why: BGP picks routes without knowing capacity, so Facebook overrides it from a controller to keep peering links from congesting.
Why withdrawn BGP routes linger as zombies during path hunting, and why withdrawing a more-specific prefix makes it worse.

main.title: More details about the October 4 outage
main.why: A backbone command cut every datacenter link, DNS servers withdrew their BGP routes, and Facebook vanished from the Internet.

main.title: A Scalable, Commodity Data Center Network Architecture
main.why: Datacenter networks relied on expensive core routers and still ran oversubscribed, so a fat-tree of cheap identical switches gives full bisection bandwidth.

main.title: Jupiter Evolving: Transforming Google's Datacenter Network via Optical Circuit Switches and Software-Defined Networking
main.why: Growing and refreshing the Clos spine was costly, so Google replaced it with optical circuit switches that link aggregation blocks directly.

main.title: Data Center TCP (DCTCP)
main.why: TCP fills switch buffers and delays short flows, so DCTCP marks ECN early and senders slow down in proportion to the marks.

main.title: Empowering Azure Storage with RDMA
main.why: Azure runs storage traffic over RDMA across whole regions to save CPU, which took PFC watchdogs, DCQCN tuning across different NICs and long-haul support.
AI training sends few, huge flows that ECMP spreads badly, so Meta's RoCE fabric splits each flow over more queue pairs and uses PFC without DCQCN.
WAN links were overprovisioned for peaks and failures, so B4's centralized traffic engineering runs them near full utilization.

further.title: B4 and After: Managing Hierarchy, Partitioning, and Asymmetry for Availability and Scale in Google's Software-Defined WAN

main.title: Orion: Google's Software-Defined Networking Control Plane
main.why: To run Google's datacenter and WAN networks from software reliably, Orion splits the control plane into microservices that share state through a pub-sub database.
Users far from Dropbox's datacenters had slow connections, so it built edge PoPs and compared anycast with GeoDNS for steering users to them.

main.title: Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Network Load Balancer
main.why: Hardware load balancers were costly and hard to scale, so Maglev runs on commodity servers with consistent hashing that keeps connections across backend changes.
nginx's per-worker connection pools forced extra handshakes to origins, so Cloudflare wrote Pingora with one pool shared across threads.
